edges.description: Dermal vessel occlusion reduces tissue perfusion and causes painful lower-extremity ulcers.
Healing of ischemic dermal microvascular ulcers produces porcelain-white atrophic scars termed atrophie blanche.
Occlusion of dermal microvessels produces livedo racemosa discoloration in the affected lower-extremity skin.
Dermal microvascular occlusion and resulting ischemic ulceration cause severe lower-extremity pain.

Thrombus formation in the vasa nervorum—analogous to microvascular thrombosis in dermal vessels—causes ischemic peripheral nerve injury, presenting as dysesthesia, hypoesthesia, axonal polyneuropathy, or mononeuritis multiplex.
PAI-1-mediated inhibition of fibrinolysis prevents dissolution of nascent intraluminal fibrin thrombi in superficial dermal microvessels.
Inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states accelerate fibrin formation and promote microvascular thrombus deposition in dermal vessels.

nodes.description: Anticoagulant treatment, including low-molecular-weight heparin or direct oral anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban, is the first-line pharmacologic approach for livedoid vasculopathy and prevents microvascular thrombus propagation.

evidence.reference_title: Characteristics, risk factors and treatment reality in livedoid vasculopathy – a multicentre analysis
evidence.snippet: The analysis of patient treatment history showed that heparin was most effective (12/17), while anti-inflammatory regimens were, although often used (17/24), not effective (0/17).

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Among them, pain management, wound care, control of cardiovascular risk factors, and both antiplatelets and anticoagulants, mostly rivaroxaban, are the main therapies used.

nodes.description: Healing ulcers leave porcelain-white atrophic scars, classically termed atrophie blanche.

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: The clinical appearance is characterized by Livedo racemosa, painful ulceration, located in the distal parts of the lower extremities, followed by healing as porcelain-white, atrophic scars, the so-called Atrophie blanche.

nodes.description: Anabolic steroid therapy with danazol (typically 200 mg/day) is the second most frequently reported monotherapy for livedoid vasculopathy; it enhances endogenous fibrinolysis, inhibits coagulation, and increases hepatic synthesis of proteins C and S.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Anabolic steroids were the second most frequently reported monotherapy for the treatment of LV (38). Danazol was the most commonly used steroid, given in a dose of 200 mg/day, although stanozolol 4 mg/day can also be used (38, 44). Systemic steroids increase fibrinolysis, inhibit coagulation, and induce hepatic synthesis of protease inhibitors (such as proteins C and S).

nodes.description: Occlusion and thrombosis of dermal vessels create local ischemia and drive the painful ulceration and atrophic scarring that characterize LV.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Histopathologically, it shows intraluminal fibrin deposition and thrombosis, segmental hyalinization, and endothelial proliferation.

nodes.id: F5 Factor V Leiden susceptibility signal

meta.association: Factor V Leiden is a reported thrombophilia association in livedoid vasculopathy cohorts (~14–18% of tested patients); this is a prothrombotic susceptibility signal rather than a monogenic disease-defining cause.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: The most common prothrombotic factors observed were antiphospholipid antibodies (17.64%), factor V Leiden mutation in heterozygosis (17.64%), and protein C and/or S deficiency (8.82%).

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: Less frequent findings were Factor V G1691A and Prothrombin G20210A polymorphism in 14% out of 135 and 11% out of 85 LV patients, respectively.

evidence.reference_title: Correlation of Genetic Polymorphism and Livedo Vasculitis
evidence.snippet: It has been reported to be associated with some gene mutations, for example, factor V Leiden gene.

nodes.description: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) delivers 100% oxygen at elevated pressure to counter dermal tissue hypoxia, promote fibrinolysis and angiogenesis, and accelerate ulcer healing and pain relief in refractory livedoid vasculopathy.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: HBOT has also been reported to be an effective alternative for LV (47, 48). HBOT releases 100% oxygen at high pressures, increasing tissue oxygenation and improving tissue ischemia. It also promotes fibrinolysis and angiogenesis, resulting in better ulcer healing (38).

nodes.description: Intravenous prostacyclin analogue therapy with iloprost is used as an add-on vasodilator and antiplatelet/microcirculatory agent when anticoagulation alone gives an insufficient therapeutic response.

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: In case of an insufficient therapeutical response, we add prostacycline-analoga such as iloprost as an intravenous therapy in a maximum dosage of 20 µg per day over 3–5 days every 4 weeks (61).

nodes.description: Elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) expression and functional SERPINE1 promoter polymorphisms (such as -675 4G/5G and A844G) inhibit endogenous plasminogen activation, impairing fibrinolytic clearance of nascent fibrin clots in superficial dermal microvessels.

evidence.reference_title: Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1: a potential etiological role in livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI)-1 is a primary inhibitory component of the endogenous fibrinolytic system in blood coagulation.

evidence.reference_title: Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1: a potential etiological role in livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Enhanced expression and genotype polymorphism of PAI-1 have been observed in LV patients.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: A recent systematic review of genetic variants in LV found that PAI-1 675 4G/5G was the most common, accounting for 85.26% of the patients, followed by PAI-1 A844G, MTHFR C677T, and MTHFR A1298C variants (17).

nodes.description: Inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states—including heterozygous factor V Leiden (F5 p.Arg506Gln) activated protein C resistance, prothrombin G20210A, protein C or S deficiency, antiphospholipid antibodies, elevated lipoprotein(a), and hyperhomocysteinemia—promote excess thrombin generation and fibrin formation in the lower-extremity dermal microcirculation.

evidence.reference_title: Characteristics, risk factors and treatment reality in livedoid vasculopathy – a multicentre analysis
evidence.snippet: Analysis of 27 patients revealed that LV patients had an increased Body Mass Index (BMI; 11/27), hypertension (19/27) and increased levels of lipoprotein (a) (5/12) and homocysteine (10/12) in the blood.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: The most common prothrombotic factors observed were antiphospholipid antibodies (17.64%), factor V Leiden mutation in heterozygosis (17.64%), and protein C and/or S deficiency (8.82%).

evidence.reference_title: Correlation of Genetic Polymorphism and Livedo Vasculitis
evidence.snippet: It has been reported to be associated with some gene mutations, for example, factor V Leiden gene.

nodes.description: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, typically 2 g/kg every 4 weeks) is a high-response alternative for refractory livedoid vasculopathy, improving pain, skin ulceration, and dysesthesia/neuropathy symptoms.

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of intravenous immunoglobulin for treating refractory livedoid vasculopathy: a systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Overall, to a certain degree, IVIG is probably a safe and effective treatment alternative for refractory LV patients, which still need to be confirmed by large-scale randomized controlled clinical trials.

nodes.description: Livedo racemosa or livedo-pattern violaceous discoloration commonly accompanies ulceration.

evidence.reference_title: Characteristics, risk factors and treatment reality in livedoid vasculopathy – a multicentre analysis
evidence.snippet: Investigation of the clinical appearance found that 82% of patients had livedo racemosa, and the ankle region was most likely to be affected by ulceration (56–70%).

nodes.description: Painful purpuric ulcers most often affect the lower legs, ankles, and feet.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Clinically, it is characterized by the presence of painful purpuric ulcers on the lower extremities.

nodes.description: Peripheral neuropathy—manifesting as dysesthesia, hypoesthesia, paresthesia, asymmetric axonal polyneuropathy, or mononeuritis multiplex—is the only known extracutaneous manifestation of livedoid vasculopathy and arises from thrombus formation in the vasa nervorum.

evidence.reference_title: A comprehensive review on pathogenesis, associations, clinical findings, and treatment of livedoid vasculopathy
evidence.snippet: Peripheral neuropathy is the only known extracutaneous manifestation of LV.

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: In a very severe form of LV patients also describe symptoms of a polyneuropathy, like dys- and hypoesthesia.

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: In contrast to other diseases associated with mononeuritis multiplex, where vasculitis can be seen in the vasa nervorum, in LV thrombus formation can be seen in the vasa nervorum comparable to thrombus formation in the dermal vessels (49, 50).

meta.association: Reported susceptibility association through PAI-1 expression or promoter polymorphism affecting fibrinolysis; not a Mendelian causal gene for LV.

evidence.snippet: Enhanced expression and genotype polymorphism of PAI-1 have been observed in LV patients.

nodes.description: Pain triggered by cutaneous ischemia from dermal vessel occlusion is a major symptom of active ulcerative LV and substantially impairs mobility and quality of life.

evidence.reference_title: Livedoid vasculopathy – A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
evidence.snippet: Occluding vasculopathy in the dermal vessels lead to ischemia and so massive pain (9, 10).

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of intravenous immunoglobulin for treating refractory livedoid vasculopathy: a systematic review.
evidence.snippet: The effective rate of IVIG therapy in LV patients was 95% (76/80) in published studies, showing a good clinical response for resolution of pain, skin ulcerations, and neurological symptoms, and reducing the dependence on glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents.
